transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I’m losing a lot of time rechecking things. My dressing supplies, the door locks, file dimensions at work, revision notes—I keep going through the same routine because I don’t feel like I can move on until I’ve checked enough times for the anxiety to settle down. It’s taking up hours.
Before you start rechecking, do you get unwanted thoughts or images that keep coming into your mind?

Yes. Even when I know I cleaned the wound area or reviewed a CAD file, this thought keeps coming back that I missed one tiny thing. Then I start thinking it could cause an infection, or a design mistake could hurt someone. I know I’ve already checked, but I can’t seem to reason the thought away.
Do these thoughts and checking feel unwanted to you?

Yes. I don’t want the thoughts or the checking. I’ll know I cleaned the wound area or reviewed the CAD file, but then this thought cuts in that I missed one tiny thing and it could cause an infection or hurt someone. I can’t seem to just reason it away.
When you start checking, is it usually because an unwanted thought suddenly pops into your mind first?
Yeah. I’ll get this feeling that I can’t move on yet, and then I start going through the same checks again—supplies, locks, work files—until the anxiety comes down. It can take hours.
If you tried not to do the checking, would your anxiety rise sharply?

Yes, a lot. If I try to stop after one check, it feels like I’m not allowed to move on. The anxiety keeps building until I go back through the supplies, locks, or work files again and again. I can lose hours doing it, just waiting for the anxiety to drop enough.
Do these unwanted thoughts also come into your mind at times when you are not checking things?

Yes. Even when I’m not checking, it can just pop in—like after I cleaned the wound area, I’ll suddenly think I missed something and it could get infected. Or with a CAD file, I’ll be doing something else and worry there’s one small mistake that could hurt someone. I know I reviewed it, but I can’t really make the thought go away.
Do you recognize these thoughts as your own thoughts, even though they feel intrusive and hard to control?

Yes. I know they’re my thoughts—it’s not like someone else is putting them there. But even after I’ve cleaned the wound area or reviewed a CAD file, I keep thinking I missed one tiny thing and it could cause an infection or hurt someone. I can’t just reason it away.
Do you feel that these fears about having missed something are excessive or unreasonable?

I mean, logically I know I cleaned it or reviewed the file. But the thought that I missed one tiny thing keeps cutting in, and then it feels like it could lead to an infection or someone getting hurt. I can’t really reason myself out of it.
When you start checking, does it usually begin because an intrusive thought like “I missed something” pops into your mind first?

Yes. I’ll get the thought that I might have missed something, and then I start checking. With the supplies, locks, or work files, I end up going through the same routine over and over because I don’t feel like I can move on until the anxiety comes down. It can take up hours.
Do these repeated checking routines feel out of line with how you want to be, rather than just your normal preferred way of doing things?

Yes. It’s not how I want to spend my time. I’m losing hours rechecking dressing supplies, door locks, file dimensions, revision notes—going through the same routine until the anxiety drops enough that I feel like I’m allowed to stop.
When the checking starts, is your main problem the intrusive thought that you missed something, or the urge to perform the checking routine itself?

It’s mostly the urge to do the checking. Once I start, I feel like I can’t move on until I’ve repeated the routine enough that the anxiety comes down. That’s what’s taking up hours—checking the supplies, locks, file dimensions, revision notes over and over.
Do you do the checking mainly to make the anxiety go down?
Yes. I keep rechecking because I need the anxiety to come down. Until I’ve gone through the supplies or locks or work details enough times, it feels like I’m not allowed to move on.
Are the intrusive thoughts themselves a major source of distress even when you are not doing the checking?

Yes. Even when I’m not checking, the thought can keep cutting in that I missed one tiny thing—like the wound area wasn’t properly cleaned, or there’s an error in a CAD file—and that it could cause an infection or hurt someone. I know I’ve reviewed it, but I can’t just reason the thought away.
Which bothers you more overall: the intrusive thought that you may have missed something, or the repeated checking itself?

The repeated checking, overall. The thought starts it, but what’s really disrupting my life is losing hours going through the supplies, locks, or work details again and again until the anxiety finally drops enough for me to stop.
Do these checking routines feel alien to the kind of person you want to be?

Yeah, they do. I don’t want to spend hours rechecking dressing supplies, locks, file dimensions, and revision notes. I want to finish something and move on, but it feels like I can’t until I’ve repeated the routine enough for the anxiety to drop.
If you stop the checking before it feels complete, do you become afraid that something bad will happen?

Yes. If I stop before it feels complete, I’m afraid I’ll have missed something and that it could lead to a problem. So I keep rechecking—supplies, locks, work files—until the anxiety comes down enough that I can finally move on.
When you are not checking, do these intrusive thoughts take up a lot of time on their own?

Yes. Even when I’m not checking, the thought keeps coming back that I missed one tiny thing. Like, I can know I cleaned a wound area or reviewed a CAD file, but I still worry it could become an infection or a design mistake that hurts someone. I can’t just reason it away.
Do you ever feel the checking is the right or satisfying way to do things, rather than something you wish you could stop?

No, it doesn’t feel satisfying. It feels like I have to do it. I lose hours going back over the supplies, locks, dimensions, and revision notes, just repeating the routine until the anxiety drops enough that I can move on.
On a typical day, do these unwanted thoughts by themselves take up more than an hour?

Yes, more than an hour. The thought keeps cutting in that I missed some tiny detail—like with a wound or a CAD file—and that it could end up hurting someone. I know I checked it, but I can’t just reason it away.
Besides checking, do you do any other repeated rituals to reduce the anxiety?

It’s mostly the rechecking. I go over the same things—dressing supplies, locks, file dimensions, revision notes—again and again. I don’t feel like I can move on until I’ve done the routine enough times for the anxiety to come down.
